extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of Shakespeare and literary chronology; literary historians
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for identifying Shakespeare's sources, assessing his reading and education, and dating and attributing his plays by external, internal, and metrical evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: External evidence for dating plays
rubrics_metrics.description: Records of the performance of plays in letters, diaries, accounts, and the like; quotation, allusion, imitation, or parody in other works; entries in the books of the Master of the Revels at Court, and in the Register of the Stationers' Company; dates on the title-pages of the plays themselves; facts and traditions about the life of the author; dates in the lives of actors and in the careers of companies known to have performed the plays, and in the histories of theaters in which they were presented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: manuscript performance of The Comedy of Errors at Gray's Inn (1594); Dr. Simon Forman's diary noting performances of Macbeth, Cymbeline, The Winter's Tale (1610–1611); Francis Meres' Palladis Tamia (1598) listing plays; pamphlets (e.g., Somers's voyage) suggesting sources for The Tempest. Use these documentary traces as the most specific external evidences for chronology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partly external/partly internal evidence (allusions as hybrid evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidences derived from allusions in the plays to current events, personal or political, and references to other books; references from one play of Shakespeare's to another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Prologue to Henry V referencing Essex's expedition to Ireland (1599); quotation from Marlowe in As You Like It; a play referring to another (promise in 2 Henry IV). Treat such references as hybrid evidence that links internal content to external datable events or publications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purely internal evidence and its limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Tests based on moral or aesthetic considerations, methods of treating plot and character, and changing characteristics of style (classical allusions and Latin words, figures of speech, diffuseness or concentration, artificiality or lifelikeness in dialogue, use of prose or verse, employment of oaths).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Internal evidence is subjective and requires careful judgment. Use plot- and character-method tests as the least subjective internal measures; treat stylistic indicators as supplementary rather than conclusive. Beware of reader bias when weighing moral/esthetic indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metrical tests for chronology and attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Tests derived from changes in versification such as the frequency of rhyme (heroic couplet, alternates, sonnet arrangements), doggerel lines, alexandrines (lines of twelve syllables), presence of an extra syllable before a pause within the line, short lines (especially at the end of speeches), substitution of other feet for iambic blank verse, weak and light endings, position of the pause in the line ('end-stopped' or 'run on'), and feminine or hypermetrical endings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These metrical features are more capable of mechanical calculation than many other tests, but still have subjective elements. The text lists specific valuable measures (e.g., frequency of rhyme, % blank verse, % run-on speeches, number of light and weak endings) and gives the example line: 'These many summers in a sea of glor-y.' Use versification patterns to corroborate external evidence and supplement other internal indicators, allowing for thematic or stylistic exception when a subject demands special metrical treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of kinds of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: A working taxonomy for dating/attribution: purely external evidence; partly external and partly internal evidence; and purely internal evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the threefold division to organize evidence: treat purely external documentary traces as primary, hybrid allusions as context-linking evidence, and internal stylistic/metrical tests as supplementary and interpretive. Recognize that each class has different degrees of specificity and reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of school-books and elementary texts as evidence of schooling
rubrics_metrics.description: Echoes of school texts (e.g., Lily's Grammar, Æsop's Fables, Sententiæ Pueriles, Distichs of Cato, Mantuanus) and elementary Latin phrases in the plays indicate what Shakespeare likely learned at the grammar school.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify specific conversational echoes, quoted lines, and topical references (e.g., phrases in Merry Wives, Henry IV, Love's Labour's Lost, Twelfth Night) and map them to known schoolbooks to argue for the contents and level of the author's schooling. Use occurrences of Latin fragments and familiarity with school curricula as indicators of elementary Latin training rather than full scholarship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inferring language proficiency from textual evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Inferences about knowledge of Greek, French, Italian, or Spanish based on passages in the plays: presence of French passages implies a working knowledge of French; many Italian and Spanish sources were used via English or French translations, so direct knowledge of those languages is not necessarily implied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between knowledge of originals and use of translations or intermediaries (e.g., Montaigne via Florio, Decameron/prototypes via English translations). Use the nature of allusions, verbatim echoes, and linguistic features to decide whether Shakespeare read an author in the original or via translation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifying literary sources and their channels
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether Shakespeare's plots and materials derive from classical authors (Ovid, Plutarch, Seneca), continental novelle (Boccaccio, Bandello, Cinthio), contemporary English translations and compilations (Painter, Holinshed, North's Plutarch, Gesta Romanorum), or contemporary dramatists (Marlowe, Kyd, Lyly, Peele).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace plots and detailed parallels to likely sources, noting when English or French translations/intermediaries were the probable channel. For historical plays, prioritize chronicles (Holinshed, Hall, Grafton, Fabyan, Stowe) and for Roman tragedies prioritize North's Plutarch. Consider the possibility of lost plays or intermediary dramatizations when exact textual matches are absent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of the Sonnets as biographical evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The Sonnets (published 1609) furnish no reliable knowledge of Shakespeare's personal affairs beyond that he wrote admiring/complimentary sonnets to a young man urged to marry and treated an intrigue with an unknown woman; attempts to identify persons (e.g., 'Mr. W. H.') have failed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the Sonnets with caution in biography: whether they are genuine and personal or conventional and literary, they should be considered in connection with the dramas and other documentary/traditional evidence rather than used alone to reconstruct personal history or emotional experiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpreting breadth and limits of 'reading' as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Shakespeare should be seen as a reader rather than a scholar—he used books for what interested him and did not study them for complete mastery; traces of many fields may reflect opportunistic, fragmentary borrowing rather than systematic erudition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When arguing from allusions to knowledge in law, medicine, navigation, theology, etc., prefer the more economical hypothesis that a man of acute mind can pick up technical matter that interests him temporarily. Avoid overstating 'professional' mastery from scattered textual echoes; consider enthusiast studies in single subjects suspect of overstretching the evidence.
